lines: A bike club orders 100 tune-ups in June: 4,000 dollars of work. You buy 1,000 dollars of parts up front, and the club pays in 60 days. On paper, June is your best month ever. In the bank, you end June at minus 50 dollars.
Profit counts a sale when you make it. Cash counts it when you get paid. Ending cash is starting cash, plus cash in, minus cash out. For June: 500, plus 1,000, minus 1,550, is minus 50.
Money customers owe you is an account receivable. Money you owe suppliers is an account payable. The club's 4,000 dollars is a receivable: profit you can't spend yet.
Payment terms say when a bill is due. Net 60 means within 60 days. So a cash forecast lists every dollar in and out, month by month, and the most important number is the lowest one.
When you lose cash every month, that's your burn rate. Runway is cash divided by burn rate. 1,200 dollars, with a 300 dollar burn, is 4 months.

To fix the gap, change the timing. Ask for a deposit, shorten your terms, get longer terms from suppliers, keep a cushion, or line up credit early. A 50 percent deposit turns June's minus 50 into 1,950 dollars.
Like a bear storing fat for winter, a business needs enough cash to last until the money arrives. Profit is an opinion. Cash is a fact.
